citation: Yoon SH, Kim KW, Goo JM, Kim DW, Hahn S. Observer variability in RECIST-based tumour burden measurements: a meta-analysis.
venue_and_status: European Journal of Cancer 53:5-15; published version; abstract read (PubMed); full text paywalled
problem: How large is reader variability in manual RECIST tumour-burden measurements on CT?
method: Random-effects meta-analysis of 95% limits of agreement (LoA) of the relative measurement difference
data: 12 studies of manual CT measurement according to RECIST
main_result: Between observers, pooled 95% LoA -22.1% to +25.4% for single-lesion longest diameters and -19.2% to +19.5% for sums of several lesions; within one observer -9.8% to +13.1% for sums; for the interval change of a single lesion between observers -31.3% to +30.3%. Inter-observer differences may exceed the 20% progression cut-off.
relevance: Anchor. Canonical reference that reader measurement noise is of the same order as the RECIST thresholds, so measurement shifts can cross category boundaries.
not_established: Measurement agreement only, no category-change rates; no pooled estimate for single-observer interval change or multi-lesion interval change; manual diameters only.

citation: Kuhl CK, Alparslan Y, Schmoee J, Sequeira B, Keulers A, Brümmendorf TH, Keil S. Validity of RECIST version 1.1 for response assessment in metastatic cancer: a prospective, multireader study.
venue_and_status: Radiology 290(2):349-356; published version; abstract read (PubMed); full text paywalled
problem: Does target-lesion selection drive inter-reader disagreement in RECIST 1.1 response categories?
method: Prospective multireader study; three radiologists read independently with dedicated response software; Fleiss kappa
data: 316 patients with metastatic cancer, 932 CT examinations (2015-2017), one centre
main_result: Same target lesions in 128/316 (41%). Concordant selection: category kappa 0.97, agreement on progression 97.7%. Discordant selection: kappa 0.58, agreement on progression 55.3%.
relevance: Anchor. With identical target lesions readers rarely disagree on progression (about 2%); lesion choice causes most disagreement. The manuscript fixes lesions, so measurement-only benchmarks are the relevant comparison.
not_established: Measurement and selection effects separated only by subgroup; no volumetry; other category rates not in the abstract.

citation: Oxnard GR, Zhao B, Sima CS, Ginsberg MS, James LP, Lefkowitz RA, Guo P, Kris MG, Schwartz LH, Riely GJ. Variability of lung tumor measurements on repeat computed tomography scans taken within 15 minutes.
venue_and_status: Journal of Clinical Oncology 29(23):3114-3119; published version (PMC3157977); methods and results read from the PMC page via a tool extraction, numbers checked against the abstract
problem: How much do diameter measurements change on immediate re-imaging when there is no true change?
method: Two CT scans minutes apart (median 8 min); three radiologists measured the target lesion side by side on both scans (longest diameter)
data: 30 NSCLC patients (33 consented), 30 target lesions, 90 lesion-reader measurement pairs
main_result: 84% of changes within +/-10%; 3% of the 90 lesion-reader changes met RECIST progression (>=20% increase) and none met partial response; median increase +4.3% and decrease -4.2%, range -23% to +31%; smaller lesions more variable.
relevance: Lesion-level 'no-change' floor for apparent category change, for comparison with the manuscript's lesion-pair reclassification rates.
not_established: Lung lesions, unidimensional, side-by-side reading; not patient-level; no volumetry or software dependence.

citation: Erasmus JJ, Gladish GW, Broemeling L, Sabloff BS, Truong MT, Herbst RS, Munden RF. Interobserver and intraobserver variability in measurement of non-small-cell carcinoma lung lesions: implications for assessment of tumor response.
venue_and_status: Journal of Clinical Oncology 21(13):2574-2582; published version; abstract read (PubMed); publisher full text returned HTTP 403
problem: How often would reader measurement variability misclassify lesion response under WHO or RECIST?
method: Five thoracic radiologists measured lesions on printed film twice, 5-7 days apart; statistical modelling of misclassification probabilities
data: 33 patients, 40 lung tumours (mean 4.1 cm)
main_result: Probability of misclassifying a tumour was highest for inter-observer measurements under progression criteria (43% bidimensional, 30% unidimensional) and lowest for intra-observer measurements under response criteria (2.5% bidimensional, 3.0% unidimensional).
relevance: Classic lesion-level (per-tumour) misclassification benchmark, the closest analogue of the manuscript's lesion-pair categories.
not_established: Modelled probabilities; computation method not read; film-based; pre-RECIST 1.1; not patient-level.

citation: Muenzel D, Engels HP, Bruegel M, Kehl V, Rummeny EJ, Metz S. Intra- and inter-observer variability in measurement of target lesions: implication on response evaluation according to RECIST 1.1.
venue_and_status: Radiology and Oncology 46(1):8-18; published version (PMC3423763), full text read (Europe PMC XML)
problem: How do intra- and inter-observer measurement differences propagate to the RECIST 1.1 overall response?
method: Four readers selected and measured target lesions at baseline and follow-up with PACS and a lesion-management software; Bland-Altman; misclassification counted against the mean of all observers
data: 20 oncology patients, thorax-pelvis CT, 320 RECIST reports
main_result: Single-lesion variability: intra-observer 4.9-9.6% (mean 5.9%), inter-observer 4.3-11.4% (mean 7.1%); variability of the change in sum of longest diameters 24%. Overall response discrepant from the multi-observer mean in 6.3% (single observer) and 12% (different observers) of cases; PACS and LMS categorisations did not differ (p = 0.513).
relevance: Patient-level benchmark for category change from measurement variability alone; early comparison of two software systems for response categories.
not_established: Small sample; misclassification relative to a multi-reader mean, not pairwise; target lesions only; software compared within a reading, not mixed across timepoints.

citation: Keil S, Barabasch A, Dirrichs T, Bruners P, Hansen NL, Bieling HB, Brümmendorf TH, Kuhl CK. Target lesion selection: an important factor causing variability of response classification in the Response Evaluation Criteria for Solid Tumors 1.1.
venue_and_status: Investigative Radiology 49(8):509-517; published version; abstract read (PubMed)
problem: Which factors drive variability of RECIST 1.1 response classification: manual vs automated measurement, 1D vs 3D, or target selection?
method: Three radiologists plus computer-assisted automated unidimensional and volumetric assessment of target lesions
data: 41 women with metastatic breast cancer; staging and first follow-up CT
main_result: Between-reader category disagreement 19/41 (46%), kappa 0.53; progressive vs non-progressive disagreement 11/41 (27%). Same target lesions: 76% agreement (19/25); different lesions: 81% disagreement (13/16). Disagreement due to manual vs automated measurement 11/41 (27%) and due to unidimensional vs volumetric measurement 6/41 (15%).
relevance: Patient-level benchmark separating measurement-method changes (automation, volumetry) from lesion selection: method changes alone moved 15-27% of patients.
not_established: Single 41-patient breast cohort; abstract only; volumetric thresholds not verified.

citation: Zhao B, Lee SM, Lee HJ, Tan Y, Qi J, Persigehl T, Mozley DP, Schwartz LH. Variability in assessing treatment response: metastatic colorectal cancer as a paradigm.
venue_and_status: Clinical Cancer Research 20(13):3560-3568; author manuscript (PMC4337392) read via NCBI E-utilities
problem: How variable are uni-, bi- and volumetric change measurements in metastatic colorectal cancer across readers and target selections?
method: Three radiologists selected and measured target lesions at baseline and 6 weeks (independent selection, and remeasurement of one reader's lesions); linear mixed models
data: 29 mCRC trial patients; 198 target lesions (liver, lung, nodes, other)
main_result: Variability of relative change with independent selection 11% (uni), 19% (bi), 22% (volume); same lesions 8%, 14%, 12%. Authors suggest variability-based cut-offs of +/-15% (SLD) and +/-30% (volume) and state that 'the spherical relationships among the cut-off values ... do not seem to exist'.
relevance: Caveat on sphere-converted thresholds; volumetric change variability in liver-dominant metastatic disease.
not_established: No category-change rates; small cohort; proposed cut-offs not validated against outcome.

citation: van Kessel CS, van Leeuwen MS, Witteveen PO, Kwee TC, Verkooijen HM, van Hillegersberg R. Semi-automatic software increases CT measurement accuracy but not response classification of colorectal liver metastases after chemotherapy.
venue_and_status: European Journal of Radiology 81(10):2543-2549; published version; abstract read (PubMed)
problem: Does semi-automatic diameter or volume software reduce variability of response classification?
method: Two observers measured each metastasis three times by manual diameter, automatic diameter and automatic volume; RECIST 1.0 categories; kappa and discordance
data: 33 patients, 138 colorectal liver metastases, pre- and post-chemotherapy CT
main_result: Inter-observer variability 4.23% (manual diameter), 2.02% (automatic diameter), 14.86% (automatic volume); classification kappa 0.653/0.548/0.548; between-observer discordance 17.8%, 22.2%, 22.2%.
relevance: Changing the measurement tool did not by itself remove category disagreement in liver metastases.
not_established: RECIST 1.0; volumetric thresholds not verified; two observers.

citation: Goldmacher GV, Goldberg CM, Boyle L, Jia L, Gause CK, Green MC, Schwartz LH. Setting the standard: empirical benchmarks for case-level site-central discordance in radiographic endpoints in oncology clinical trials.
venue_and_status: Contemporary Clinical Trials Communications 53:101682; published version (open access, PMC13571531), full text read (Europe PMC XML)
problem: What case-level discordance between investigator and blinded central RECIST 1.1 assessments should be expected?
method: Pooled 2x2 analysis of investigator vs BICR progression and objective response; Clopper-Pearson CIs
data: 39 phase 1b-3 pembrolizumab-based trials, 12 tumour types; PD n = 20,908; confirmed OR n = 21,520
main_result: Discordance 17.7% (95% CI 17.2-18.2) for PD, 12.2% for confirmed OR, 14.7% for unconfirmed OR; PD discordance from 11.8% (melanoma) to 22.8% (HCC); 17.3% with vs 20.2% without real-time verification of progression.
relevance: Largest current benchmark for how often two reading processes disagree on progression per patient, including melanoma.
not_established: Whole RECIST (lesion selection, non-target and new lesions, clinical information), not measurement alone; immunotherapy trials; up to 10 target lesions allowed; read platforms not standardised; no adjudication data.

citation: Beaumont H, Iannessi A. Can we predict discordant RECIST 1.1 evaluations in double read clinical trials?
venue_and_status: Frontiers in Oncology 13:1239570; published version (open access); abstract read (PubMed)
problem: How frequent are double-read discrepancies in central review of lung trials, and can they be predicted?
method: Retrospective analysis of BICR double reads in five trials; risk factors; machine-learning prediction
data: 1724 lung-cancer patients, 17 radiologists, five immunotherapy or targeted-therapy trials
main_result: Average discrepancy rates 21.0% (PD declared), 41.0% (date of PD), 28.8% (best overall response), 48.8% (date of first response); rates rose over trial time; prediction from baseline data was poor.
relevance: Reader-to-reader benchmark for progression and best-response disagreement in central review.
not_established: Includes lesion selection and new lesions; lung only; measurement-only share not separated.

citation: Siegel MJ, Ippolito JE, Wahl RL, Siegel BA. Discrepant assessments of progressive disease in clinical trials between routine clinical reads and formal RECIST 1.1 interpretations.
venue_and_status: Radiology: Imaging Cancer 5(5):e230001; published version; abstract read (PubMed; PMC page blocked by a browser check)
problem: How often do routine clinical reads disagree with formal RECIST 1.1 core-laboratory reads on progression, and why?
method: Retrospective comparison of routine clinical interpretations with local core-laboratory RECIST 1.1 interpretations using lesion-tracking software
data: 1053 trial patients (January-July 2021); 327 with PD on at least one read
main_result: PD agreement 65% (213/327); routine reads over-called PD in 32% (105/327) and under-called in 3% (9/327); over-calls due to erroneous target-lesion measurement in 58% (61/105), non-target errors 30%, new-lesion misclassification 11%; 93% (98/105) of over-called patients remained on trial for at least one cycle.
relevance: Links measurement error to a decision (removal from trial or therapy); measurement was the main cause of false progression.
not_established: Single institution; the formal read is not ground truth; most consequences were averted by the core-laboratory read.

citation: Smesseim I, Bucho TT, Tissier R, van der Mierden S, Lalezari F, Burgers JA, Trebeschi S. Assessing the reliability of Response Evaluation Criteria In Solid Tumors (RECIST): a systematic review of the factors contributing to inter-observer variability.
venue_and_status: Insights into Imaging 17(1):180; published version (open access, PMC13319625), full text read (Europe PMC XML)
problem: Which factors contribute to inter-observer variability (IOV) in RECIST?
method: Systematic review with nine factor classes (manual vs semi-automatic, lesion selection, 1D vs 2D/3D, intra-reader, experience, local vs central, criteria variants, imaging type, follow-up schedule)
data: 88 included studies (246 assessed); median sample 50 patients
main_result: IOV is affected mainly by measurement method, lesion selection and image quality; all but one of 19 manual-vs-semi-automatic studies found lower IOV with semi-automatic tools (exception van Kessel 2012); heterogeneous statistics prevent pooling.
relevance: Single current review for RECIST variability factors; its taxonomy contains no software- or model-version factor.
not_established: No pooled category-change rate; nothing on software or model versions or AI updates.

citation: Heiselman JS, Horvat N, El Homsi M, Agridag-Ucpinar B, Yildirim O, Gonen M, Ecker BL, O'Reilly EM, Drebin JA, Balachandran VP, et al. Image registration improves inter-reader agreement of objective response in CT assessment of pancreas adenocarcinoma.
venue_and_status: European Journal of Radiology 199:112776; published version; abstract read (PubMed)
problem: How reproducible is CT response assessment of pancreatic adenocarcinoma during neoadjuvant therapy?
method: Two senior and two junior radiologists segmented and measured tumours at baseline and restaging; RECIST 1.1 and WHO; with and without image-registration assistance
data: 30 resectable PDAC patients from a phase II trial
main_result: Low agreement on segmented volumes (generalised conformity 0.43 baseline, 0.38 restaging); response kappa 0.0 (junior), 0.37 (senior), 0.23 (all readers); registration-assisted response kappa 0.81.
relevance: Pancreas-specific evidence that response categories are fragile to measurement; context for the PanTrack cohort.
not_established: Primary tumours in the neoadjuvant setting, not hepatic metastases; small; abstract only.

citation: Zimmermann M, Kuhl CK, Engelke H, Bettermann G, Keil S. Factors that drive heterogeneity of response-to-treatment of different metastatic deposits within the same patients as measured by RECIST 1.1 analyses.
venue_and_status: Academic Radiology 28(8):e235-e239; published version; abstract read (PubMed)
problem: How often do different metastases in one patient respond differently enough to change progressive vs non-progressive disease?
method: Three readers with dedicated response software; patients for whom readers chose different target sets; PD vs non-PD
data: 355 patients with metastatic disease; 200 with different target sets
main_result: Clinically significant heterogeneity of response (different PD vs non-PD depending on target set) in 67/200 (34%).
relevance: Supports the manuscript's caveat that lesion-level categories are not patient-level response, and motivates the per-patient sum.
not_established: Reader disagreement used as a proxy for biological heterogeneity; no volumetry.

citation: Mantatzis M, Kakolyris S, Amarantidis K, Karayiannakis A, Prassopoulos P. Treatment response classification of liver metastatic disease evaluated on imaging. Are RECIST unidimensional measurements accurate?
venue_and_status: European Radiology 19(7):1809-1816; published version; abstract read (PubMed)
problem: Do RECIST diameters and volumes classify liver-metastasis response alike, per patient and per lesion?
method: RECIST and volume measurements of target lesions on three MRI examinations during chemotherapy; kappa
data: 44 patients with new liver lesions; 77 patient comparisons; 301 lesion classifications
main_result: Agreement in 64/77 patient comparisons and 253/301 lesion classifications (kappa 0.735 and 0.741); methods differed in 16.88% of comparisons; 27.6% of target lesions did not follow their patient's response category; actual volumes differed from sphere volumes of the same diameter.
relevance: Direct evidence that lesion-level categories diverge from the patient-level category in about a quarter of lesions, and that sphere volumes misstate real volumes.
not_established: MRI not CT; thresholds not verified; small sample.

citation: Mozley PD, Bendtsen C, Zhao B, Schwartz LH, Thorn M, Rong Y, Zhang L, Perrone A, Korn R, Buckler AJ. Measurement of tumor volumes improves RECIST-based response assessments in advanced lung cancer.
venue_and_status: Translational Oncology 5(1):19-25; published version (open access, PMC3281412); methods and results read from the PMC page via a tool extraction
problem: Are volumes more reproducible than longest diameters, and would volume-based response differ from RECIST?
method: Seven independent teams with their own semi-automated tools measured volumes and longest diameters; Janson-Olsson iota; volume cut-offs from +/-2 SD of measurement variability
data: 10 advanced lung-cancer patients, 13 target lesions, 71 time points, 6461 measurements
main_result: Inter-team agreement higher for volumes than diameters (iota 0.945 vs 0.734); with variability-based cut-offs (about -25%/+25%) volumes met partial response in 9/10 vs 3/10 (automated SLD) and progression in 8/10 vs 4/10; volumes would have shortened PFS by a mean of 62 +/- 47 days in 8 of 9 growing patients; authors project earlier management changes.
relevance: Anchor for volumetric response; a multi-tool study (different software per team).
not_established: Did not use -65%/+73% RECIST-equivalent thresholds; 10 patients; 'earlier management change' is a projection, not observed; no outcome validation.

citation: Prasad SR, Jhaveri KS, Saini S, Hahn PF, Halpern EF, Sumner JE. CT tumor measurement for therapeutic response assessment: comparison of unidimensional, bidimensional, and volumetric techniques - initial observations.
venue_and_status: Radiology 225(2):416-419; published version; abstract read (PubMed); full text paywalled
problem: Do 1D, 2D and volumetric criteria classify patient response alike?
method: Two radiologists; per-patient sums of all lesion measurements; partial response >30% (1D), >50% (2D), >65% (volume) decrease; progression >20%, >25%, >73% increase
data: 38 patients with breast-cancer liver metastases in a phase III trial; baseline and 6-month CT
main_result: 1D and 2D categories concordant in 37/38; volumetric category differed from 1D in 12 and from 2D in 13 patients (6 PR to SD, 2 SD to PR, 4 PD to SD by volume).
relevance: Primary precedent for applying -65%/+73% volume equivalents to per-patient sums of lesion volumes, as the revision proposes.
not_established: Small cohort; manual tracing; no outcome comparison; abstract only.

citation: Gong AJ, Ruchalski K, Kim HJ, Douek M, Gutierrez A, Patel M, Sai V, Coy H, Villegas B, Raman S, et al. RECIST 1.1 target lesion categorical response in metastatic renal cell carcinoma: a comparison of conventional versus volumetric assessment.
venue_and_status: Radiology: Imaging Cancer 5(5):e220166; published version (open access, PMC10546365); methods and results read from the PMC page via a tool extraction
problem: Does the spherical approximation of RECIST agree with measured target-lesion volumes?
method: Vmodel (sphere from each RECIST diameter) vs Vactual (manual contours), summed over target lesions; -65%/+73% extrapolated from RECIST with a spherical model; 5 mm rule not applied; McNemar and kappa
data: Metastatic renal cell carcinoma trial: 638 patients at baseline, 593 at week 9, 508 at week 17
main_result: Vmodel-sum labelled PD in 52 vs Vactual-sum 31 patients at week 9 (57 vs 39 at week 17); 25/52 (48%) Vmodel-PD were SD by actual volume; kappa 0.63 (week 9) and 0.70 (week 17). Authors state that RECIST PD 'commonly results in the cessation of therapy'.
relevance: Best inspected evidence that the sphere conversion itself shifts patient-level categories; also states the decision consequence of a PD call.
not_established: No outcome data; the abstract reports P < .001 for overall discordance while the results give P = .017 (week 9) and P = .053 (week 17); renal cancer only.

citation: Zhao B, Obuchowski N, Yang H, Chou Y, Ma H, Guo P, Tang Y, Schwartz L, Sullivan D. Comparing quantitative imaging biomarker alliance volumetric CT classifications with RECIST response categories.
venue_and_status: Radiology Advances 2(1):umaf001; published version (open access, PMC11739520), full text read (Europe PMC XML)
problem: Do QIBA volumetric change classifications and RECIST-equivalent volume cut-offs agree with RECIST categories?
method: Three radiologists segmented lesions at baseline and follow-up with two semi-automated tools; lesion-level classification; QIBA cut-offs +/-24, 29 or 39% by baseline size; 'RECIST CTvol' cut-offs -65%/+73%; predefined disagreement types
data: 478 lesions (158 lung, 170 liver, 150 lymph node) in 281 patients from 10 historical trials; 2390 measurements
main_result: QIBA CTvol agreed with RECIST in 66.6% of interpretations (substantive disagreement 1.5%); RECIST CTvol (-65%/+73%) agreed in 86.1% and disagreed in 13.9% (6.6% substantive, 7.3% attributable to volumetric sensitivity); segmentation tool (p = .331) and scanner vendor did not predict disagreement.
relevance: Closest lesion-level benchmark to the manuscript: lesion categories from RECIST-equivalent volume thresholds vs diameter RECIST; tool choice did not predict disagreement when held fixed across timepoints.
not_established: RECIST used as reference without outcome; side-by-side segmentation; no AI segmentation; tool held fixed across timepoints.

citation: Winter KS, Hofmann FO, Thierfelder KM, Holch JW, Hesse N, Baumann AB, Modest DP, Stintzing S, Heinemann V, Ricke J, et al. Towards volumetric thresholds in RECIST 1.1: therapeutic response assessment in hepatic metastases.
venue_and_status: European Radiology 28(11):4839-4848; published version; abstract read (PubMed); full text paywalled
problem: Which volume changes correspond empirically to the RECIST -30%/+20% thresholds in liver metastases?
method: Semi-automatic diameters and volumes; loess regression of volume change on diameter change for 1, <=2 and <=5 lesions; sensitivity analyses
data: 348 metastatic colorectal cancer trial patients, 629 liver metastases, 4773 value pairs (<=2 lesions)
main_result: Volumetric thresholds -65.3% (for -30%) and +64.6% (for +20%); proposed +/-65%; concordance with RECIST 88.3% for progression and 85.0% for response.
relevance: Empirical alternative to the sphere-derived +72.8% progression threshold; supports a sensitivity analysis at +65%.
not_established: Colorectal liver metastases only; derived to mimic RECIST, not outcome; abstract only.

citation: Vogel MN, Schmücker S, Maksimovic O, Hartmann J, Claussen CD, Horger M. Reduction in growth threshold for pulmonary metastases: an opportunity for volumetry and its impact on treatment decisions.
venue_and_status: British Journal of Radiology 85(1015):959-964; published version (PMC3474043); methods and results read from the PMC page via a tool extraction
problem: Does automated volumetry change response categories and treatment decisions compared with RECIST?
method: Automated volumetry (OncoTREAT, MeVis) vs manual RECIST; three methods: RECIST, volume equivalents -65%/+73%, variability-based +/-38%
data: 58 patients, 203 pulmonary metastases under chemotherapy; University Hospital Tübingen
main_result: 15/58 (17%) inconsistent with at least one method; theoretical impact on treatment decisions in 8 (13%); RECIST vs volume equivalents diverged in 6 patients (kappa 0.79), 5 with a theoretical decision impact.
relevance: Patient-level volume-equivalent precedent from the Longitudinal-CT source centre, with an explicit decision-impact estimate.
not_established: Decision impact judged theoretically, not observed; lung metastases; software version not reported.

citation: Rothe JH, Grieser C, Lehmkuhl L, Schnapauff D, Fernandez CP, Maurer MH, Mussler A, Hamm B, Denecke T, Steffen IG. Size determination and response assessment of liver metastases with computed tomography - comparison of RECIST and volumetric algorithms.
venue_and_status: European Journal of Radiology 82(11):1831-1839; published version; abstract read (PubMed)
problem: How do volumetric algorithms and RECIST compare for size and response of liver metastases?
method: Three 3D segmentation algorithms vs RECIST (with volume from the largest diameter); triplicate measurements by one observer; follow-up response comparison
data: 102 liver metastases in 45 patients (22 pancreatic, 23 colon cancer); follow-up of 55 metastases in 29 patients
main_result: RECIST-based volumes larger by 0.4-41.1%; intra-observer variability higher for RECIST and threshold segmentation (3.6-32.8%) than for slice-based or region-growing segmentation (0.4-13.7%); response classification discordant in 10-21% of patients depending on algorithm and thresholds.
relevance: Only inspected study including pancreatic-cancer liver metastases (as in PanTrack) that compares algorithm-dependent response categories.
not_established: One observer; small follow-up subset; thresholds not verified from the abstract.

citation: Zimmermann M, Kuhl C, Engelke H, Bettermann G, Keil S. Volumetric measurements of target lesions: does it improve inter-reader variability for oncological response assessment according to RECIST 1.1 guidelines compared to standard unidimensional measurements?
venue_and_status: Polish Journal of Radiology 86:e594-e600; published version (open access, PMC8634421), full text read (Europe PMC XML)
problem: Do summed target-lesion volumes (vRECIST) change categories and reduce inter-reader disagreement?
method: The same three readers re-measured their target lesions volumetrically; patient-level sum of volumes; PD >= +73%, PR <= -65% (attributed to RECIST guidelines, Therasse 2000); PD vs non-PD
data: 50 patients selected because three readers had discordant PD vs non-PD with unidimensional RECIST
main_result: Per reader, uRECIST and vRECIST agreed in 66%, 84% and 88% of patients (12-34% changed); inter-reader agreement 0% (uRECIST, by selection) vs 36% (vRECIST).
relevance: Precedent for patient-level sums of volumes with -65%/+73%.
not_established: Enriched for discordant cases, so rates do not generalise; manual interpolated volumes.

citation: Wesdorp NJ, Bolhuis K, Roor J, van Waesberghe JHTM, van Dieren S, van Amerongen MJ, Chapelle T, Dejong CHC, Engelbrecht MRW, Gerhards MF, et al. The prognostic value of total tumor volume response compared with RECIST1.1 in patients with initially unresectable colorectal liver metastases undergoing systemic treatment.
venue_and_status: Annals of Surgery Open 2(4):e103; published version (open access); abstract read (PubMed)
problem: Is total tumour volume (TTV) response more prognostic than RECIST 1.1 in colorectal liver metastases?
method: TTV from segmentation software vs RECIST 1.1 at baseline and follow-up; TTV thresholds 10, 20 and 40%; recurrence-free survival
data: 210 patients (CAIRO5 trial), 420 CT scans, 7820 liver metastases
main_result: RECIST and TTV change discordant in 30-50% of patients depending on threshold; TTV decrease >40% in 47 (22%) RECIST-stable patients; in 118 resected patients, <10% TTV decrease predicted shorter RFS (P = .015) while RECIST did not (P = .821).
relevance: Patient-level total volume can classify differently from RECIST and may carry prognostic information in liver metastases.
not_established: No established TTV threshold; subgroup analysis; not a RECIST-equivalent threshold study.

citation: Lubner MG, Stabo N, Lubner SJ, del Rio AM, Song C, Pickhardt PJ. Volumetric versus unidimensional measures of metastatic colorectal cancer in assessing disease response.
venue_and_status: Clinical Colorectal Cancer 16(4):324-333.e1; published version; abstract read (PubMed)
problem: Do volumetric categories predict survival better than unidimensional ones?
method: Three readers; semi-automated 1D and 3D measures at three time points; RECIST 1.1 thresholds for 1D and volume; Cox and Kaplan-Meier
data: 105 metastatic colorectal cancer patients
main_result: 1D and 3D both separated PD from SD/PR and neither separated SD from PR; survival stratification similar; volumetric reproducibility comparable.
relevance: Counter-evidence that volumetric categories do not always outperform diameters for outcome.
not_established: Single centre; volumetric thresholds not verified from the abstract.

citation: Dahm IC, Kolb M, Altmann S, Nikolaou K, Gatidis S, Othman AE, Hering A, Moltz JH, Peisen F. Reliability of automated RECIST 1.1 and volumetric RECIST target lesion response evaluation in follow-up CT - a multi-center, multi-observer reading study.
venue_and_status: Cancers 16(23):4009; published version (open access, PMC11640155), full text read (Europe PMC XML)
problem: Are fully automated RECIST 1.1 and volumetric RECIST from an nnU-Net plus registration pipeline reliable against three radiologists?
method: Automated lesion tracking and segmentation; diameters and volumes from masks; volumetric RECIST -65%/+73%; ICC, Fleiss and Cohen kappa at lesion and patient level
data: 58 stage IV melanoma patients (Tübingen registry, baseline 2015-2018), 114 preselected target lesions; three readers from three institutions
main_result: Reader timepoint-response agreement Fleiss kappa 0.68-0.79; mean manual vs automated diameter categories Cohen kappa 0.67-0.76; automated diameter vs automated volume kappa 0.81; volumetric RECIST differed from diameter RECIST in 7/58 patients (3 involving PD); major PD/non-PD deviations across all assessments in 10/58 (3 near threshold, 5 missed or mismeasured lesions, 4 of them by the algorithm, 2 non-spherical shapes).
relevance: Same disease and centre as the Longitudinal-CT cohort, automated nnU-Net volumes and the same threshold convention; patient-level benchmark for automated vs manual and volume vs diameter categories.
not_established: Preselected target lesions; no new lesions; one model version; no version-change or reprocessing analysis; overlap with Longitudinal-CT patients not verifiable.
code_or_data: data on request; code under a materials transfer agreement

citation: de Grauw MJJ, Westphal M, Smit EJ, Scholten ET, Loßau T, Moltz J, Bottazzi S, Cuocolo R, D'Angelo A, George AB, et al. Multicenter AI- versus expert-assisted RECIST target lesion measurements in follow-up body CT of patients with cancer.
venue_and_status: Radiology Advances 3(5):umag028; published version (open access, PMC13588574), full text read (Europe PMC XML; Appendix C not read)
problem: Does AI assistance for follow-up RECIST target-lesion measurement change reading time and response consistency?
method: Retrospective multireader crossover; baseline target lesions premeasured; follow-up remeasured unassisted, AI-assisted (nnU-Net-based proposals) or expert-assisted; Bayesian GLMMs; SLD-based target-lesion outcome agreement
data: 212 patients, 539 target lesions, two Dutch hospitals; 23 readers from 11 institutions
main_result: Patient-level target-lesion outcome agreement 72.5% unassisted vs 80.4% AI-assisted (+7.7 percentage points, 95% CI 2.8-12.7); expert-assisted +13.3 points; AI raised lesion-level deviation from the expert mean (+1.32 mm) and cut reading time by 36 s per patient.
relevance: Recent benchmark: about one in four patient readings disagree on the target-lesion category when only the follow-up is remeasured; a mixed-source design (fixed human baseline, assisted follow-up).
not_established: Agreement definition detailed in Appendix C (not read); target lesions only; readers told all proposals were AI; no version comparison.
code_or_data: model not public; analysis code on request

citation: Joskowicz L, Szeskin A, Rochman S, Dodi A, Lederman R, Fruchtman-Brot H, Azraq Y, Sosna J. Follow-up of liver metastases: a comparison of deep learning and RECIST 1.1.
venue_and_status: European Radiology 33(12):9320-9327; published version; abstract read (PubMed); full text paywalled
problem: Does deep-learning volumetric change analysis improve disease-status classification of liver metastases compared with RECIST 1.1 reading?
method: Two radiologists read prior/current CT pairs conventionally and with a DL-aided volumetric lesion-change report; reference from expert-validated DL segmentation
data: 43 patients, 86 CT studies, 1041 liver metastases
main_result: Disease-status classification differed from the reference in 40/86 (46.5%) conventional readings vs '10 out of 86 (27.9%)' computer-aided readings (as printed); differences driven mainly by lesion-volume differences.
relevance: AI volumetric follow-up of liver metastases changes disease-status classification; same group as the cited SimU-Net work (Szeskin 2023).
not_established: Abstract count and percentage are inconsistent (10/86 = 11.6%); reference derived from the DL output (circularity); full text not read.

citation: Abbas M, Andrade-Miranda G, Bourbonne V, Jaouen V, Lepage C, Aparicio T, Visvikis D, Badic B, Conze PH. AI-driven volumetric approach for automatic chemotherapy response assessment in colorectal liver metastases.
venue_and_status: European Radiology 36(10):7490-7501; published version; abstract read (PubMed)
problem: Does AI volumetric response of colorectal liver metastases stratify survival better than RECIST 1.1?
method: nnU-Net trained on 476 CT scans; AI-volumetric vs RECIST 1.1 response at 3 months; overall survival
data: 157 patients from the PRODIGE 9-FFCD trial; 112 held-out scans for segmentation
main_result: Dice 0.775 (0.566 for small lesions); both methods prognostic overall (p < .0001); in liver-only disease (n = 43) volumetric response was prognostic (p = .015 at -30%) while RECIST was not (p = .21).
relevance: Automated volumetric response is being proposed for decisions in liver metastases; small-lesion errors are the weak point.
not_established: Subgroup of 43; thresholds not RECIST-equivalent; no reproducibility across model versions.

citation: Leszczyńska A, Seweryn M, Obuchowicz R, Strzelecki M, Piórkowski A, Potocki PM. Artificial intelligence for RECIST-based radiologic treatment response assessment in solid tumors: a systematic review of imaging- and report-derived approaches.
venue_and_status: Cancers 18(5):808; published version (open access); abstract read (PubMed)
problem: How well do AI methods assign RECIST categories, and how strong is the evidence?
method: PRISMA systematic review (search 6 December 2025) of studies in which AI directly assigned RECIST categories against a reference
data: 4 eligible studies (2 image-based, 2 report-based)
main_result: Image-based pipelines (nnU-Net, 3D U-Net) reached classification accuracy 0.77 with kappa 0.60 against manual reference, and kappa 0.67-0.81 for RECIST measurements; evidence sparse and heterogeneous; external validation lacking.
relevance: Supports a statement that evidence on AI-assigned response categories is still sparse and silent on model updates.
not_established: Very few studies; nothing on version changes or longitudinal compatibility.

citation: Adhikary S, Chabi N, Mastmeyer A. How errors from prompt-assisted longitudinal tumour segmentation change RECIST 1.1 target-lesion response categories: a retrospective out-of-fold analysis.
venue_and_status: Research Square preprint, version 1 posted 10 August 2026, not peer reviewed; full PDF read
problem: How often do follow-up segmentation errors of a prompt-assisted longitudinal model change RECIST 1.1 target-lesion categories, and through which error types?
method: LongiSeg (nnU-Net residual-encoder backbone, public autoPET branch) given the expert baseline mask and location prompts; held-out-fold checkpoints; mask-derived target-lesion RECIST (SLD, -30%/+20% with 5 mm rule); Shapley attribution of disagreements
data: Longitudinal-CT (autoPET/CT IV Task 2) metastatic melanoma cohort, Tübingen; 258 response-evaluable patients, 683 target lesions
main_result: Target-lesion category disagreed with the expert-mask reference in 43/258 patients (16.7%, Wilson 95% CI 12.6-21.7; kappa 0.76); contributions: sizing 8.3%, detection/localisation 5.2%, false persistence 3.1%; boundary shifts of -1 mm/+1 mm gave 8.5%/14.0% flip rates; 15.5-17.8% across nine threshold pairs.
relevance: Closest neighbour: same dataset as the manuscript's internal cohort; patient-level RECIST category change from mixed measurement sources (expert baseline, model follow-up).
not_established: Not a version or update study; one model; expert baseline always; target-lesion component only; diameters not volumes; preprint.
code_or_data: LongiSeg public on GitHub (autoPET branch); analysis code not distributed

citation: US Food and Drug Administration (CDER and CBER). Clinical Trial Imaging Endpoint Process Standards: Guidance for Industry.
venue_and_status: FDA guidance, final version April 2018 (docket FDA-2011-D-0586); full PDF read
problem: How should imaging-based trial endpoints be acquired, interpreted and quality controlled?
method: Regulatory guidance (nonbinding recommendations) on imaging charters
data: not applicable
main_result: Charters should specify important imaging equipment including software; ongoing control of hardware and software versions may matter in quantitative imaging; 'Software upgrades within the trial period may affect how images are generated. Changes in an image may be caused by these software changes and be incorrectly attributed to actual clinical changes'; computer-assisted interpretation and QC of critical software functions should be described; the same computer-assisted interpretation tool should be available to all readers.
relevance: Regulatory recognition that within-trial software changes can be mistaken for clinical change; nearest regulatory analogue of version mixing (overlaps T6).
not_established: Addresses image generation/processing and reading tools, not versions of segmentation models; no quantitative guidance.

citation: Seymour L, Bogaerts J, Perrone A, Ford R, Schwartz LH, Mandrekar S, Lin NU, Litière S, Dancey J, Chen A, et al. iRECIST: guidelines for response criteria for use in trials testing immunotherapeutics.
venue_and_status: Lancet Oncology 18(3):e143-e152; author manuscript (PMC5648544) read via NCBI E-utilities
problem: How should RECIST be adapted for immunotherapy trials with atypical responses?
method: RECIST Working Group consensus guideline
data: not applicable
main_result: Introduces unconfirmed and confirmed progression (iUPD, iCPD); states that 'early discontinuation of an effective drug is not desirable' while 'continued long-term treatment with a non-effective drug past true progression might delay the initiation of potentially effective salvage therapy'; treatment beyond RECIST progression only for clinically stable patients.
relevance: Authoritative statement of the two-sided cost of a wrong progression call; melanoma is the classic setting.
not_established: Concerns biological pseudoprogression, not measurement error; no quantified costs.

citation: Hodi FS, Hwu WJ, Kefford R, Weber JS, Daud A, Hamid O, Patnaik A, Ribas A, Robert C, Gangadhar TC, et al. Evaluation of immune-related response criteria and RECIST v1.1 in patients with advanced melanoma treated with pembrolizumab.
venue_and_status: Journal of Clinical Oncology 34(13):1510-1517; published version; abstract read (PubMed)
problem: How often does RECIST 1.1 call progression in melanoma patients who are not progressing by immune-related criteria, and how do they fare?
method: KEYNOTE-001 central review per irRC and RECIST 1.1
data: 655 melanoma patients; 592 surviving >=12 weeks; 327 with >=28 weeks of imaging
main_result: 84/592 (14%) had PD by RECIST 1.1 but not by irRC; 2-year OS 77.6% (non-PD by both), 37.5% (PD by RECIST only), 17.3% (PD by both); pseudoprogression in 7% of 327; RECIST might underestimate benefit in about 15% and lead to premature cessation.
relevance: Melanoma-specific evidence that a differing progression call changes who stops effective therapy.
not_established: About criteria and biology, not measurement error; post hoc; one drug.

citation: Cowell GW, Roche J, Noble C, Stobo DB, Papanastasiou A, Kidd AC, Tsim S, Blyth KG. Discordance in pleural mesothelioma response classification and modelling of impact on clinical trials.
venue_and_status: Lung Cancer 221:109624; published version; abstract read (PubMed)
problem: What does inter-radiologist discordance in response classification do to trial power and endpoint precision?
method: Multicentre retrospective discordance study (mRECIST 1.1) plus in silico two-arm trials with misclassification 0-100% (10,000 repeats each)
data: 172 chemotherapy-treated pleural mesothelioma cases from four UK centres
main_result: Discordance 35% (60/172), kappa 0.456; at 17% single-reader misclassification, power fell from 80% to 39% (ORR), 54% (DCR), 64% (PFS) and 64% (OS); endpoint coverage fell to 85-92%; 83% of discordances were intrinsic to mRECIST interpretation or measurement.
relevance: Quantifies how a misclassification rate translates into lost trial power: the decision-impact link the co-author asked for.
not_established: Mesothelioma and mRECIST; simulation assumptions; not about software or volumetry.

citation: Hong S, Schmitt N, Stone A, Denne J. Attenuation of treatment effect due to measurement variability in assessment of progression-free survival.
venue_and_status: Pharmaceutical Statistics 11(5):394-402; published version; abstract read (PubMed)
problem: How does tumour-measurement variability affect the PFS hazard ratio and median?
method: Simulation of trials with scan measurement variability and different assessment frequencies
data: simulated data
main_result: Measurement variability attenuates the treatment-effect hazard ratio towards 1, more so with frequent scans, inflating type II error; authors recommend minimising variability or enlarging samples.
relevance: Mechanistic support that non-differential measurement error biases PFS comparisons toward the null.
not_established: Simulation only; does not model systematic (directional) shifts such as a version bias.
